items.abstract: Abstract Recent years have seen a decisive turn in neuroscience toward embodiment, shifting focus from a brain-bound view of the mind to a more holistic one where the body is treated as constitutive of self and consciousness. While this turn has yielded valuable insights through studies on interoception, multisensory integration and bodily ownership, it also carries significant theoretical and ethical risks. This essay identifies the body problem: the risk of collapsing selfhood into bodyhood, with troubling consequences when applied to bodies that are marginalized or that otherwise do not meet the status quo. Tracing historical debates on mind–body relations, clarifying contemporary notions of the self and examining empirical findings on embodiment, it is argued that strong formulations of the embodied self risk reviving old reductions whereby “less body” implies “less self,” not because such formulations explicitly assert the inference, but because they leave it available for others to make. Such reductions threaten to undermine the value of persons whose bodies diverge from normative assumptions. Rather than rejecting embodiment research, this essay calls for caution against its uncritical extension, underscoring the need to guard against theoretical slippage that may entail harmful social consequences.
items.title: The Body Problem: Cautionary Notes on the Embodied Self

items.abstract: Abstract Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can expose interpretable features in language-model activations, but public SAE resources such as GemmaScope and Llama Scope are trained on generic web text rather than cybersecurity evidence. CyberLens is a purpose-trained SAE and heuristic taxonomy-mapping pipeline for cybersecurity interpretability of an open-weight language model. Because cyber uplift is a foreseeable deployment risk, reasonable care requires developers of general-purpose language models to provide proportionate internal observability of cyber-relevant behaviour. We train a width-4096 JumpReLU SAE on layer 8 of EleutherAI/pythia-160 m, a 12-layer, 162-million-parameter model with a 768-dimensional residual stream, using 14,925 documents (approximately 1.85 million tokens) of MITRE ATT&CK descriptions and procedure examples, NVD vulnerability reports, CISA KEV records, CAPEC, malware reports, phishing emails, and Dolly-15k benign contrasts, with grouped splitting to prevent source-document leakage. The cybersecurity SAE achieves FVU 0.0435 (95.7% explained variance) versus 0.186 for a matched generic-text SAE—an absolute explained- variance gain of 14.2 percentage points on the reported activation sample. Its 4,096 feature rows are mapped heuristically to ATT&CK techniques and CISSP domains using local all-MiniLM-L6-v2 similarity, with confidence scores from 0.313 to 0.928; the top 50 remain pending hand-verification after a labelling pilot failed. Refusal is 0.000 in both arms (a Pythia-160 M base model without instruction tuning or RLHF). Suppressing 20 selected features increases keyword-flagged cyber content from 0.067 to 0.317 overall and from 0.050 to 0.800 for exploit items; phishing and malware are null, and 15 of 20 exploit placeholders contain “Exploit,” inflating this lexical metric. English-only, phishing-heavy corpus; one completed layer-8 width-4,096 SAE whose observed $$L_0=286$$ greatly exceeds the target 20; heuristic, unverified labels; keyword-based outcomes; a placeholder-heavy 60-prompt intervention set; no evidence about frontier models or effective cyber-content suppression. SAE weights, feature dictionary, loader, and an interactive demonstration are released for reproducible small-model research; scaling to larger models remains future work.
items.title: Cyberlens: taxonomy-mapped sparse autoencoders for cybersecurity interpretability of open-weight language models

items.abstract: Abstract The Gettier problem suggests that the core challenge for theories of knowledge lies in eliminating knowledge-undermining epistemic luck. In response, two major approaches have emerged in contemporary epistemology: modalism and explanationism. However, both approaches have limitations and exhibit an interesting theoretical symmetry: while modalism effectively handles environmental luck, it struggles with certain cases of intervening luck; explanationism faces the reverse difficulty. This symmetrical limitation suggests that any theory of knowledge relying on a single dimension is likely to be inadequate. To address this, this paper presents a new, integrated approach – Modal Explanationism (ME). ME requires that a belief counts as knowledge just in case it is explained by the truth of the believed proposition in the actual world, and that this explanatory connection is preserved across a range of nearby possible worlds. It is argued that ME offers a more successful solution to the Gettier problem than either modalism or explanationism alone.
items.title: A Modal Explanationist Solution to the Gettier Problem

items.abstract: Abstract The Article analyzes how gender markers on passports are used to bolster the digital racial borders of the European Union (EU). It traces the history of gender markers on passports, showing that they increasingly emerged in the EU and elsewhere as part of border digitalization processes from the 1980s onward. It further investigates how gender markers on passports increasingly serve border-related risk assessments by examining the ongoing expansion of Advanced Passenger Information, Passenger Name Records, and the Visa Information System in the EU. While this analysis shows that gender markers help to identify the “unwanted” migrant—a deeply racialized concept—the Article also interrogates whether abolishing gender markers would necessarily render borders gender- or race-neutral. It therefore explores how border governance that relies on big data and biometric tools, rather than gender markers, may equally reinforce cisnormative and racialized borders.
items.title: Gender Markers in Passports and the Digital Racial Borders of the European Union

items.abstract: Abstract This paper aims to advance current debates on gendered language reform by making explicit the assumptions in much of the philosophical literature, and by proposing a reorientation of how we theorize about pronoun reform and linguistic amelioration. While sympathetic to the normative aims of prominent proposals, I caution that prescriptions grounded in any single language risk overstating language-specific features and blurring the sources and dynamics of gender essentialism. Drawing on the case of Mandarin Chinese, where gendered pronouns were a modern invention, I clarify the limits of language-specific diagnoses and show how reform is mediated by social conditions of uptake. More broadly, I advocate a shift from language-specific proposals to a cross- and trans-linguistic perspective: cross-linguistic comparison identifies which claims generalize across languages, and a trans-linguistic lens highlights how reform ideas and practices travel across contexts and are reshaped through uptake and negotiation. This approach offers a more philosophically robust account of the prospects and limits of linguistic amelioration, and of language’s role in social change.
items.title: Pronouns and Linguistic Amelioration
Shmuel Nili, Beyond the Law’s Reach? Powerful Criminals, Foreign Entanglement, and Justice in the Shadow of Violence. (New York: Oxford University Press, 2024.)
Una reflexión a doce años de “Comparative Matters”, de Ran Hirschl

items.abstract: ABSTRACT This article focuses on the question of how to understand the role and use of ethical theories in bioethics. Work in bioethics often involves uses of ethical theory, but methodological developments such as the empirical turn and the growing insights into the plurality and contextuality of moral considerations challenge a traditional view of ethical theories as providing moral input into the value‐neutral descriptions offered by empirical studies. Nevertheless, bioethics is characterised by a relative neglect of questions related to the use of ethical theories. The article develops a number of desiderata that any understanding of the role of ethical theories should be able to address; to accommodate moral plurality and contextuality, to motivate choices and uses of specific theories, to minimise risks of theory‐driven attention and blindness, to allow for theoretical plurality, to address relations between theories and theoretical integrity. It then presents some challenges for existing accounts of theory‐use in bioethics, thus paving the way for an alternative understanding of the role of ethical theories in bioethics. The suggestion presented here is that ethical theories should be understood as descriptions or representations of moral grammars , implicit normative structures of thinking and action that constitute moral considerations. Furthermore, in relation to problems in bioethics, it is suggested that ethical theories are used as heuristic tools to illuminate and clarify moral grammars as they appear in specific bioethical poblems or studies.
items.title: Reconsidering the Role of Ethical Theories in Bioethics: Ethical Theories as Heuristic Descriptions of Moral Grammars

items.abstract: Ulrike Kern (2016) unpacks the history of a concept, broken colors. Though it’s been in use since the early seventeenth century, and is even used today by painters, critics, and art theorists when discussing color, it hasn’t much influenced philosophy. Instead, it evolved independently, alongside the early modern philosophical discussions of color. This paper has two goals. First, work out a philosophical reconstruction of the concept whose early history Kern so ably traces. So, this paper is a philosophical contribution to the history of ideas. The paper’s second goal is to show how broken colors contribute to two contemporary issues. First, they help us understand the depiction of things as colored, and second, they can deepen our understanding of the nature of chromatic experience. Broken colors are thus relevant to contemporary philosophy of art and perception. Though there are historically informed contemporary accounts of color on the market—Adams (2016) stands out—they typically address the history of philosophical discussions of color. And there is comparatively little work in the philosophy of art about the depiction of things as colored.
items.title: Understanding Broken Colors

items.abstract: Can we offer a constitutive account of fittingness? Offering such an account has proven difficult because of the great diversity of fit-assessable responses—e.g., believing, desiring, fearing, blaming, apologizing, thanking, and laughing. Yet, when surveying such examples of fit-apt  responses, what's striking is that invariably each response-type has a job, a goal, an end, a telos. Believing, desiring, fearing, blaming, apologizing, thanking, and laughing are all plausible candidates for having proper functions. The account I aim to defend runs with this idea. Put roughly, fittingness is the relation that holds between a response and its object just when and because the object has the properties that an object of that response needs to possess for the response to non-deviantly fulfill its function.
items.title: A Function-Based Account of Fittingness

items.abstract: The concept of essence is a paradigm case of a putatively hyperintensional concept in metaphysics, a concept that can draw distinctions between necessarily equivalent propositions. Yet as several authors have recently emphasized, fine-grained distinctions in metaphysics come with a substantial risk of inconsistency, due to the Russell-Myhill paradox and its variants. This concern is especially pressing for hyperintensionalists about essence because the hyperintensionality of essence has been motivated primarily by examples. This paper presents a novel, more systematic case for the hyperintensionality of essence that shows that the relevant distinctions can be systematically modeled in a natural theoretical framework. I start by offering a general heuristic to motivate a range of examples of fine-grained essentialist distinctions. I then present a higher-order logical framework for regimenting essentialist statements and provide a general argument for hyperintensionality on the basis of minimal assumptions about the logic of essence. Finally, I address the question of consistency by developing a semantic framework that demonstrates that the relevant fine-grained distinctions can indeed be consistently drawn.
items.title: Essence and Grain

items.abstract: I propose a novel A-theory that attractively articulates our common-sense, pre-relativistic conception of time. This A-theory posits fundamental facts about how things were at a specific past times. It treats time’s passing by positing fundamental facts like: four hours passed from 8am today until noon. It allows fundamental cross-temporal relationships. I show that the presentism–eternalism dilemma does not embarrass the proposed A-theory. There are two notions of existence in play: existence at a time and ‘∃-existence’. Neither features in the fundamental facts. I define them up in a way that vindicates the claims of common sense. Past objects count as metaphysically ‘gone’, but there are fundamental facts about how they were. My account rejects presentism and eternalism (properly defined). I defend other aspects of the proposal elsewhere.
items.title: Escape the Presentism–Eternalism Dilemma: Towards A Common-Sense A-Theory

items.abstract: Human cognition and behavior are guided by a myriad of norms which enable us to successfully navigate our social environment and our interactions with others. Many of these norms might be hard for us to articulate (e.g. how far to sit or stand from a stranger on the bus), and some of them differentiate between different hierarchies and roles, reflecting patterns of injustice. This paper addresses the fact that social norms, including gendered, ableist, adultist, and racist norms, influence our perception of action possibilities, or affordances, making some actions possible for some agents and not for others. In particular, we propose an account of these interactions in terms of scripts, that is, expected sequences of actions that shape the landscape of the possible ways to interact with one another. Scripts can be learned implicitly, they are dynamic and flexible, and can regulate complex interactions by prescribing permissible actions and responses in specific situations. A script-based account can explain the way norms regulate which actions we perceive as possible in a representationalist way, and can help us explain how norm change occurs.
items.title: Seeing what to do: norms, scripts, and social affordances
